'''abligate†''' (ab′li-gāt), ''v. t.'' [< L. ''ab,'' from, + ''ligatus,'' pp. of ''ligare,'' tie: see ''lien'' and ''obligate.''] To tie up so as to hinder. ''Bailey.''

'''abligation†''' (ab-li-gā′shọn), ''n.'' The act of tying up so as to hinder. ''Smart.''

''abliguritio(n-),'' also written ''abligurritio(n-),'' a consuming in feasting, < ''abligurrire,'' consume in feasting, lit. lick away, < ''ab,'' away, + ''ligurrire,'' lick, be dainty, akin to ''lingere,'' lick, and E. ''lick,'' q. v.] Excess; prodigal expense for food. [Rare.]

'''ablins,''' ''adv.'' See ''aiblins.''

'''ablocation''' (ab-lō-kā′shọn), ''n.'' A letting for hire; lease.

'''abloom''' (a-blöm′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.'' [< ''a''<sup>3</sup>, ''prep.,'' + ''bloom''<sup>1</sup>.] In a blooming state; in blossom.

¶
'''abode'''<sup>2</sup> (a-bōd′). Preterit of ''abide''<sup>1</sup>.

'''abode'''<sup>3</sup>† (a̤-bōd′), ''n.'' [< ME. ''abode'', < ''abeden'' (pp. ''aboden''), < AS. ''ābeódan'': see ''a-''<sup>1</sup> and ''bode''<sup>2</sup>.] An omen; a prognostication; a foreboding.
{{smaller block|Astrologicall and other like vaine predictions and ''abodes''.
{{right|''Lydgate.''}}
High-thund’ring Juno’s husband stirs my spirit with true ''abodes''. {{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, xiii. 146.}}}}

'''abode'''<sup>3</sup>† (a-bōd′), ''v.'' [< ''abode''<sup>3</sup>, ''n.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To foreshow; prognosticate; forebode.
{{smaller block|<poem>This tempest,
Dashing the garment of this peace, ''aboded''
The sudden breach on’t.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., i. 1.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To be an omen; forebode: as, “this ''abodes'' sadly,” ''Dr. H. More'', Decay of Christian Piety.

'''abodement'''† (a̤-bōd′mẹnt), ''n.'' [< ''abode''<sup>3</sup> + ''-ment''.] Foreboding; prognostication; omen.
{{smaller block|Tush, man! ''abodements'' must not now affright us.
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., iv. 7.}}}}

'''aboding'''† (a̤-bō′ding), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''abode''<sup>3</sup>. Cf. ''boding''.] Presentiment; prognostication; foreboding: as, “strange ominous ''abodings'' and fears,” ''Bp. Bull'', Works, II. 489.

'''abogado''' (ä-bọ̄-gä′dō), ''n.'' [Sp., < L. ''advocatus'': see ''advocate''.] An advocate; a counselor: used in parts of the United States settled by Spaniards.

'''aboideau, aboiteau''' (a-boi-dō′, -tō′), ''n.'' [Of uncertain F. origin.] A dam to prevent the tide from overflowing a marsh. [New Brunswick.]

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|ablewhackets|14|aboil}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''ablewhackets''' (ā′bl-whak-ets), ''n.'' [< ''able'' (uncertain, perhaps alluding to ''able seaman'') + ''whack.''] A game of cards played by sailors, in which the loser receives a whack or blow with a knotted handkerchief for every game he loses. Also spelled ''abelwhackets.''

'''abligate†''' (ab′li-gāt), ''v. t.'' [< L. ''ab,'' from, + ''ligatus,'' pp. of ''ligare,'' tie: see ''lien'' and ''obligate.''] To tie up so as to hinder. ''Bailey.''

'''abligation†''' (ab-li-gā′shọn), ''n.'' The act of tying up so as to hinder. ''Smart.''

'''abligurition''' (ab-lig-ū-rish′ọn), ''n.'' [< L. ''abliguritio(n-),'' also written ''abligurritio(n-),'' a consuming in feasting, < ''abligurrire,'' consume in feasting, lit. lick away, < ''ab,'' away, + ''ligurrire,'' lick, be dainty, akin to ''lingere,'' lick, and E. ''lick,'' q. v.] Excess; prodigal expense for food. [Rare.]

'''ablins,''' ''adv.'' See ''aiblins.''

'''ablocate''' (ab′lō-kāt), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''ablocated,'' ppr. ''ablocating.'' [< L. ''ablocatus,'' pp. of ''ablocare,'' let out on hire, < ''ab,'' from, + ''locare,'' let out, place: see ''locate.''] To let out; lease.

'''ablocation''' (ab-lō-kā′shọn), ''n.'' A letting for hire; lease.

'''abloom''' (a-blöm′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.'' [< ''a''<sup>3</sup>, ''prep.,'' + ''bloom''<sup>1</sup>.] In a blooming state; in blossom.

'''ablude†''' (ab-löd′), ''v. i.''; pret. and pp. ''abluded,'' ppr. ''abluding.'' [< L. ''abludere,'' be different from, < ''ab,'' from, + ''ludere,'' play. Cf. Gr. ἀπᾴδειν, sing out of tune, dissent, < ἀπό (= L. ''ab''), from, + ᾄδειν, sing.] To be unlike; differ; be out of harmony. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The wise advice of our Seneca not much ''abluding'' from the counsel of that blessed apostle.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Balm of Gilead, vii. 1.}}}}

'''abluent''' (ab′lö-ent), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< L. ''abluen(t-)s'', ppr. of ''abluere'', wash off, cleanse, < ''ab'', off, + ''luere'' = Gr. λούειν, wash.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Washing; cleansing; purifying.

'''II.''' ''n.'' In ''med.'': (''a'') That which purifies the blood, or carries off impurities from the system, especially from the stomach and intestines; a detergent. (''b'') That which removes filth or viscid matter from ulcers or from the skin.

'''ablution''' (ab-lö′shon), ''n.'' [< ME. ''ablution'', ''ablucioun'', < OF. ''ablution'', < L. ''ablutio(n-)'', < ''abluere'', wash off: see ''abluent'', ''a.''] 1. In a general sense, the act of washing; a cleansing or purification by water.—2. Any ceremonial washing. {{smaller|(''a'') Among the Oriental races, a washing of the person or of parts of it, as the hands and face, and among the Hebrews also of garments and vessels, as a religious duty on certain occasions, or in preparation for some religious act, as a sign of moral purification, and sometimes in token of innocence of, or absence of responsibility for, some particular crime or charge (whence the expression “to wash one’s hands of anything”). The Mohammedan law requires ablution before each of the five daily prayers, and permits it to be performed with sand when water cannot be procured, as in the desert.}}
{{smaller block|There is a natural analogy between the ''ablution'' of the body and the purification of the soul.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Worthy Communicant.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') In the ''Rom. Cath. Ch.'': (1) The washing of the feet of the poor (John xiii. 14) on Maundy or Holy Thursday, called ''mandatum''. (2) The washing of the celebrant’s hands before and after communion. (''c'') In the ''Eastern Church'', the purification of the newly baptized on the eighth day after baptism.}}

'''3.''' In the ''Rom. Cath. Ch.'', the wine and water which after communion are separately poured into the chalice over the thumb and index-finger of the officiating priest, who drinks this ablution before going on with the closing prayers.—'''4'''†. In ''chem.'', the purification of bodies by the affusion of a proper liquor, as water to dissolve salts.—'''5.''' In ''med.'', the washing of the body externally, as by baths, or internally, by diluent fluids.—'''6.''' The water used in cleansing.
{{smaller block|<poem>Wash’d by the briny wave, the pious train
Are cleansed, and cast the ''ablutions'' in the main.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, i. 413.}}}}

'''ablutionary''' (ab-lö′shọn-ạ̄-ri), ''a.'' Pertaining to ablution.

'''abluvion''' (ab-lö′vi-ọn), ''n.'' [< ML. ''abluvio(n-)'', a changed form of L. ''abluvium'', a flood or deluge, < ''abluere'', wash off: see ''abluent'', ''a.''] '''1'''†. A flood.—'''2.''' That which is washed off or away. ''Dwight.'' [Rare.]

'''ably''' (ā′bli), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''abeliche'', < ''abel'', able, + ''-liche'', -ly<sup>2</sup>.] In an able manner; with ability.

'''-ably.''' [< ''-able'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>, ME. ''abel-liche''; so ''-bly'', ''-ibly''.] The termination of adverbs from adjectives in ''-able''.

'''abnegate''' (ab′nẹ̄-gāt), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''abnegated'', ppr. ''abnegating''. [< L. ''abnegatus'', pp. of ''abnegare'', refuse, deny, < ''ab'', off, + ''negare'', deny: see ''negation''.] To deny (anything) to one’s self; renounce; give up or surrender.
{{smaller block|The government which . . . could not, without ''abnegating'' its own very nature, take the lead in making rebellion an excuse for revolution.
{{right|''Lowell'', Study Windows, p. 167.}}}}

'''abnegation''' (ab-nē-gā′shọn), ''n''. [< L. ''abnegatio(n-)'', denial, < ''abnegare'', deny: see ''abnegate''.] The act of abnegating; a renunciation.
{{smaller block|With ''abnegation'' of God, of his honour, and of religion, they may retain the friendship of the court.
{{right|''Knox'', Letter to Queen Reg. of Scot.}}}}
{{smaller block|Judicious confirmation, judicious ''abnegation''.
{{right|''Carlyle'', The Diamond Necklace.}}}}

'''abnegative''' (ab′nē-gā-tiv or ab-neg′a̤-tiv), ''a''. Denying; negative. ''Clarke''. [Rare.]

'''abnegator''' (ab′nē-gā-tọr), ''n''. [L., a denier.] One who abnegates, denies, renounces, or opposes. ''Sir E. Sandys''.

'''abnerval''' (ab-nėr′va̤l), ''a''. [< L. ''ab'', from, + ''nervus'', nerve.] From or away from the nerve. {{smaller|Applied to electrical currents passing in a muscular fiber from the point of application of a nerve-fiber toward the extremities of the muscular fiber.}}

'''abnet''' (ab′net), ''n''. [< Heb. ''abnēt'', a belt.] 1. In ''Jewish antiq''., a girdle of fine linen worn by priests. Also called ''abanet''.
{{smaller block|A long array of priests, in their plain white garments overwrapped by ''abnets'' of many folds and gorgeous colors.
{{right|''L. Wallace'', Ben-Hur, p. 530.}}}}

2. In ''surg''., a bandage resembling a Jewish priest’s girdle.

'''abnodate†''' (ab′nọ̄-dāt), ''v. t.'' [< L. ''abnodatus'', pp. of ''abnodare'', cut off knots, < ''ab'' (= E. ''off'') + ''nodare'', fill with knots, < ''nodus'' = E. ''knot'': see ''node'' and ''knot.''] To cut knots from, as trees. ''Blount.''

'''abnodation†''' (ab-nọ̄-dā′sho̤n), ''n.'' The act of cutting away the knots of trees.

'''abnormal''' (ab-nôr′ma̤l), ''a.'' [< L. ''abnormis'', deviating from a fixed rule, irregular, < ''ab'', from, + ''norma'', a rule: see ''norm'' and ''normal.'' Earlier ''anormal'', q. v.] Not conformed or conforming to rule; deviating from a type or standard; contrary to system or law; irregular; unnatural.
{{smaller block|An argument is, that the above-specified breeds, though agreeing generally in constitution, habits, voice, colouring, and in most parts of their structure, with the wild rock pigeon, yet are certainly highly ''abnormal'' in other parts of their structure. {{right|''Darwin'', Origin of Species, i.}}}}
'''Abnormal dispersion.''' {{smaller|See ''dispersion.''}}

'''Abnormales''' (ab-nôr-mā′lēz), ''n. pl.'' [NL., pl. of ''abnormalis'': see ''abnormal.''] In ''ornith.'', in Garrod’s and Forbes’s arrangement of ''Passeres'', a division of the ''Oscines'' or ''Acromyodi'' established for the Australian genera ''Menura'' and ''Atrichia'', the lyre-bird and scrub-bird, on account of the abnormal construction of the syrinx. See ''Atrichiidæ'' and ''Menuridæ.''

'''abnormality''' (ab-nôr-mal′ị-ti), ''n.'' [< ''abnormal'' + ''-ity.''] 1. The state or quality of being abnormal; deviation from a standard, rule, or type; irregularity; abnormity.
{{smaller block|The recognition of the ''abnormality'' of his state was in this case, at any rate, assured. {{right|''Mind'', IX. 112.}}}}

2. That which is abnormal; that which is characterized by deviation from a standard, rule, or type; an abnormal feature.
{{smaller block|The word [vice], in its true and original meaning, signifies a fault, an ''abnormality''. {{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XXVI. 234.}}}}
{{smaller block|A single [human] body presented the extraordinary number of twenty-five distinct ''abnormalities''.
{{right|''Darwin'', Descent of Man, I. 105.}}}}

'''abnormally''' (ab-nôr′mạl-i), ''adv.'' In an abnormal manner.
{{smaller block|Impressions made on the retina ''abnormally'' from within, by the mind or imagination, are also sometimes projected outward, and become the delusive signs of external objects having no existence. {{right|''Le Conte'', Sight, p. 72.}}}}

'''abnormity''' (ab-nôr′mị-ti), ''n.'' [< ''abnormous'' + ''-ity'', on type of ''enormity'', < ''enormous''.] Irregularity; deformity; abnormality.
{{smaller block|Blonde and whitish hair being, properly speaking, an ''abnormity''. {{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XXII. 67.}}}}
{{smaller block|The faradaic current which cures some deep-seated ''abnormity'' of nutrition. {{right|''J. Fiske'', Cos. Phil., I. 302.}}}}

'''abnormous''' (ab-nôr′mus), ''a.'' [< L. ''abnormis'', with suffix ''-ous'', like ''enormous'', < L. ''enormis'': see ''abnormal''.] Abnormal; misshapen.
{{smaller block|The general structure of the couplet through the 17th century may be called ''abnormous''.
{{right|''Hallam'', Lit. Hist., IV. 251.}}}}

'''aboard'''<sup>1</sup> (a̤-bōrd′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' and ''prep.'' [< ME. ''on borde'', < AS. ''on borde'' (dat.), ''on bord'' (acc.): prep. ''on'', on; ''bord'', plank, side of a ship: see ''board''. Cf. F. ''aller à bord'', go aboard; D. ''aan boord gaan'', go aboard. The F. ''à bord'' has merged in the E. phrase. Cf. ''aboard''<sup>2</sup>.]

'''I.''' ''adv.'' '''1.''' On the deck or in the hold of a ship or vessel; into or upon a vessel. [In the U. S. used also of railroad-cars and other vehicles.]
{{smaller block|He lowdly cald to such as were ''abord.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. vi. 4.}}}}

'''2.''' Alongside; by the side; on one side.
{{smaller block|He was desirous of keeping the coast of America ''aboard.''
{{right|''Cook'', Voyages.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Aboard main tack!''' (''naut.''), an order to haul one of the lower corners of the mainsail down to the chess-tree.—'''All aboard!''' the order to go on board or enter, upon the starting of a vessel or (U. S.) railroad-train.—'''To fall aboard of,''' to come or strike against: said of a ship which strikes against another broadside on or at an obtuse angle. Such a collision is distinctively called an ''abordage.''—'''To get aboard,''' to get foul of, as a ship.—'''To go aboard,''' to enter a ship; embark.—'''To haul aboard''' (''naut.''), to haul down the weather-clew of the fore or main course by the tack to the bumkin or deck.—'''To keep the land''' or '''coast aboard''' (''naut.''), to keep within sight of land while sailing along it.}}
{{smaller block|We sailed leisurely down the coast before a light fair wind, ''keeping the land'' well ''aboard.''
{{right|''R. H. Dana, Jr.'', Before the Mast, p. 124.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To lay aboard''' (''naut.''), to run alongside of, as an enemy’s ship, for the purpose of fighting.}}

'''II.''' ''prep.'' '''1.''' On board; into.
{{smaller block|We left this place, and were again conveyed ''aboard'' our ship.
{{right|''Fielding'', Voyage to Lisbon.}}}}

'''2.''' Upon; across; athwart. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Nor iron bands ''aboard''
The Pontic sea by their huge navy cast.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Virgil’s Gnat, l. 46.}}}}

'''aboard'''<sup>2</sup>† (a̤-bōrd′), ''n.'' [< F. ''abord'', approach, < ''aborder'', approach the shore, land, approach, accost (cf. ''à bord'', on board), < ''à'' (< L. ''ad''), to, + ''bord'', edge, margin, shore, < D. ''boord'', edge, brim, bank, board (of a ship): see ''aboard''<sup>1</sup>.] Approach. Also spelled ''abord.''
{{smaller block|He would, . . . at the first ''aboard'' of a stranger, . . . frame a right apprehension of him.
{{right|''Sir K. Digby'', Nat. of Bodies, p. 253.}}}}

'''abocock'''†, '''abococked'''†, ''n.'' Corrupt forms of ''bycocket.'' Compare ''abacot.''

'''abodance'''† (a̤-bō′da̤ns), ''n.'' [< ''abode''<sup>3</sup> + ''-ance.''] An omen.
{{smaller block|Verbum valde ominatum, an ill ''abodance.''
{{right|''T. Jackson'', Works, II. 635.}}}}

'''abode'''<sup>1</sup> (a̤-bōd′), ''n.'' [< ME. ''abood'', ''abod'', earlier ''abad'', continuance, stay, delay, < ME. ''abiden'' (pret. ''abod'', earlier ''abad''), abide: see ''abide''<sup>1</sup>.] 1. Stay; continuance in a place; residence for a time.
{{smaller block|I was once in Italy myself, but I thank God my ''abode'' there was only nine days.
{{right|''Ascham'', quoted by Lowell, Study Windows, p. 406.}}}}
2. A place of continuance; a dwelling; a habitation.
{{smaller block|But I know thy ''abode'', and thy going out, and thy coming in.{{right|2 Ki. xix. 27.}}}}
3†. Delay: as, “fled away without ''abode,''” ''Spenser.''—'''To make abode''', {{smaller|to dwell or reside.}} = '''Syn.''' {{smaller|2. Residence, dwelling, habitation, domicile, home, house, lodging, quarters, homestead.}}

'''abode'''<sup>2</sup> (a-bōd′). Preterit of ''abide''<sup>1</sup>.

'''abode'''<sup>3</sup>† (a̤-bōd′), ''n.'' [< ME. ''abode'', < ''abeden'' (pp. ''aboden''), < AS. ''ābeódan'': see ''a-''<sup>1</sup> and ''bode''<sup>2</sup>.] An omen; a prognostication; a foreboding.
{{smaller block|Astrologicall and other like vaine predictions and ''abodes''.
{{right|''Lydgate.''}}
High-thund’ring Juno’s husband stirs my spirit with true ''abodes''. {{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, xiii. 146.}}}}

'''abode'''<sup>3</sup>† (a-bōd′), ''v.'' [< ''abode''<sup>3</sup>, ''n.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To foreshow; prognosticate; forebode.
{{smaller block|<poem>This tempest,
Dashing the garment of this peace, ''aboded''
The sudden breach on’t.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., i. 1.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To be an omen; forebode: as, “this ''abodes'' sadly,” ''Dr. H. More'', Decay of Christian Piety.

'''abodement'''† (a̤-bōd′mẹnt), ''n.'' [< ''abode''<sup>3</sup> + ''-ment''.] Foreboding; prognostication; omen.
{{smaller block|Tush, man! ''abodements'' must not now affright us.
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., iv. 7.}}}}

'''aboding'''† (a̤-bō′ding), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''abode''<sup>3</sup>. Cf. ''boding''.] Presentiment; prognostication; foreboding: as, “strange ominous ''abodings'' and fears,” ''Bp. Bull'', Works, II. 489.

'''abogado''' (ä-bọ̄-gä′dō), ''n.'' [Sp., < L. ''advocatus'': see ''advocate''.] An advocate; a counselor: used in parts of the United States settled by Spaniards.

'''aboideau, aboiteau''' (a-boi-dō′, -tō′), ''n.'' [Of uncertain F. origin.] A dam to prevent the tide from overflowing a marsh. [New Brunswick.]

'''aboil''' (a-boil′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.'' [< ''a''<sup>3</sup>, ''prep.'', + ''boil''<sup>2</sup>.] In or into a boiling state.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
